design_detail: Phase 3, investigator-led, multisite, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trial (1:1, stratified by sex at birth and by a PHQ-9 depression score of 10 or more) at six government-run outpatient alcohol and other drug clinics in Australia (Wollongong, Geelong, Townsville, Perth, Brisbane, Adelaide), 16 November 2022 to 1 May 2025, sponsored and coordinated by the University of New South Wales. 344 adults with DSM-5 moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder were randomized and the 339 who received trial medication were analysed. Study condition: mirtazapine 30 mg each evening for 12 weeks, or matching placebo, followed by a 28-day taper; no protocolised psychosocial treatment (participants were free to use other services). Primary end point: change from baseline to week 12 in self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days (timeline follow-back), analysed with a negative binomial mixed model (condition by time). ANZCTR ACTRN12622000235707.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder treated at public outpatient clinics, 12 weeks of mirtazapine reduced self-reported days of methamphetamine use compared with placebo, and how often it caused adverse effects and stopping of the medication over those 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether mirtazapine reduced use as measured by drug tests (the oral-fluid measure did not differ); whether any benefit lasts beyond the 12 weeks of treatment (no later follow-up is reported); whether it improves depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour, quality of life or functioning (none differed); its effect in people taking antidepressants, pregnant people or people with a suicide attempt in the past year (all excluded); or rare and long-term harms (172 people treated for 12 weeks).

sample.recruitment: Mainly social media, flyers at health services and word of mouth; telephone screening, then a face-to-face eligibility assessment at the trial clinic, where participants were enrolled as patients; A$50 (US$35.59) per assessment. Of 1267 assessed, 923 were excluded (475 declined or could not be recontacted, 419 did not meet the inclusion criteria, 29 incomplete screening) (Methods › Procedures, pp. 582–583; Figure 1, p. 583).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 18 to 65; DSM-5 moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder in the past year; methamphetamine use at least twice a week in the past 4 weeks; a positive drug screen for amphetamines. Excluded: prescribed antidepressant medication; suicide attempt in the past year; pregnancy or lactation; need for acute medical care; inpatient treatment; incarceration; contraindications to mirtazapine. Detailed criteria are only in the eMethods (Supplement 3, not read) (Methods › Participants, p. 582).
sample.demographics: Mean age 42.0 (SD 8.6); 126 women (37.2%); 16% born outside Australia; median 10 years of schooling; 179 (52.8%) unemployed; 136 (40%) with a prison history; mean duration of methamphetamine use 21 years; median 24 (IQR 17 to 28) of the past 28 days used at baseline; injecting methamphetamine 48.5% (placebo) vs 43.0% (mirtazapine); PHQ-9 of 10 or more at eligibility 82 (49.1%) vs 83 (48.3%) (Abstract › Results, p. 581; Table 1, p. 584; Results › Participants, pp. 584–585).
sample.attrition: Five people randomized to placebo never received medication (3 did not attend the baseline visit, 1 was incarcerated, 1 withdrew consent) and are excluded from every analysis. Medication was discontinued by 36 of 167 (22%) on placebo and 49 of 172 (28%) on mirtazapine (P = .14); week-12 outcome data were available for 293 of 339 (86%: 88% on mirtazapine, 85% on placebo). Reasons in Figure 1: chose to stop because they did not like the medication's effects or did not feel it was working, 19 (placebo) vs 29 (mirtazapine); adverse events or other health risks, 4 vs 10 (Figure 1, p. 583; Results › Participants, p. 584; Table 3, p. 586).
sample.selection_effects: Participants sought treatment enough to enrol at a clinic but were recruited mainly by advertisement and paid for assessments. Use was heavy and long-standing (median 24 of 28 days; mean 21 years). People taking prescribed antidepressants or with a suicide attempt in the past year were excluded, which removes part of the depressed population the authors aim to generalize to. About three in four people assessed were not enrolled. 'Routine clinical practice' here still includes research assessments, electronic pill bottles and payments.

exposure.measurement: Assigned trial medication: mirtazapine or matching placebo tablets (placebo supplied by Syntro Pty Ltd), taken by mouth each evening, dispensed in bottles of 35 tablets fitted with MEMS caps and replaced at weeks 4 and 8. Clinicians could offer a half-tablet rescue dose to people who stopped for tolerability reasons (8 participants: 6 on mirtazapine, 2 on placebo). Adherence: percentage of days in the 12 weeks on which the bottle was opened (Methods › Procedures and End Points, pp. 582–583; Results › Participants, p. 584).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 30 mg daily by mouth for 12 weeks, then a taper at 15 mg for 28 days from week 12. MEMS adherence: median 52% (IQR 26% to 78%) overall and 62% (40% to 81%) when periods after discontinuation are excluded; adherence by arm is not reported in the article (Results › Participants, p. 584).
exposure.polysubstance: Days of other substance use, summed over tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, inhalants and heroin, at baseline mean 35.8 (SD 20.5) on placebo vs 33.5 (19.2) on mirtazapine (Table 1, p. 584); the arms did not differ in days of other substance use during the trial (Results › Exploratory End Points, p. 586; estimates only in eTable 2, not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants were using at entry, and the outcome is use during treatment.

comparison.controls: Matching placebo tablets on the same schedule, with the same referral information, harm-reduction brochure, assessments and payments; both arms were free to use other drug treatment and health services.
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1, stratified by sex at birth and by PHQ-9 score of 10 or more. The article does not describe how the sequence was generated or how allocation was concealed (protocol in Supplement 1, not read). Baseline characteristics were similar (Table 1, p. 584): mean days of use in the past 28 days 22.0 (placebo) vs 23.1 (mirtazapine) (Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, p. 585).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; days of other substance use similar at baseline (Table 1, p. 584).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days by timeline follow-back at baseline and weeks 4, 8 and 12, with week 12 the primary end point. Secondary: PHQ-9 (depression), Athens Insomnia Scale 5-item version, HIV Risk-Taking Behavior Scale of the Opiate Treatment Index, EQ-5D-5L utility score, and methamphetamine-negative oral fluid (cut-off 25 ng/mL) at weeks 4, 8 and 12. Exploratory: suicide risk (C-SSRS screener score of 3 or more), days of other substance use, adherence. Safety: participant-reported adverse events coded by MedDRA system organ class (Methods › End Points, p. 583).
outcomes.validity_norms: The timeline follow-back is cited as 88% sensitive and 96% specific against urine tests in earlier work; in this trial, self-reported use over the past 3 days had 89% sensitivity and 83% specificity against methamphetamine-positive oral fluid (Methods › End Points, 1st paragraph, p. 583). The oral-fluid test is objective but detects only recent use.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a larger fall in self-reported use days from baseline to week 12 on mirtazapine than on placebo (the condition-by-time interaction of a negative binomial mixed model with a random intercept and time as a factor), reported as a mean difference in days and as an incidence rate ratio; the average over weeks 4, 8 and 12 is a further estimand (Methods › Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors state that the width of confidence intervals was not adjusted for multiple comparisons (Statistical Analysis, p. 583). The count of 8 covers the primary end point, five secondary end points and two exploratory end points named in the Methods; each was estimated at weeks 4, 8 and 12 or as an average, and subgroup interactions by sex and by depression come on top.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: all clinicians, researchers and investigators were blinded to allocation (Methods › Trial Design, p. 582). The primary outcome is the participant's own report to a blinded researcher. No check of blinding is reported in the article, although drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine and could have revealed allocation.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (339 analysed): change in days of use from baseline to week 12, −7.0 (95% CI −8.5 to −5.6) on mirtazapine vs −4.8 (−6.2 to −3.4) on placebo; treatment estimand −2.2 days of 28 (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02; incidence rate ratio 0.89 (0.80 to 0.98). Week 4: −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6), P = .20; week 8: −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06; average over the 12 weeks: −1.8 (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03. Secondary at week 12: methamphetamine-negative oral fluid 12.0% vs 13.2% (difference 1.3 percentage points, −4.7 to 7.2; P = .68); PHQ-9 −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0); AIS-5 −0.6 (−1.4 to 0.2); HIV risk −0.3 (−1.0 to 0.3); EQ-5D 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9). Editors' calculation (baseline mean plus mean change; approximate, because the changes are model estimates): about 16.1 vs 17.2 days of use in the past 28 days at week 12. Editors' calculation from the counts in Table 3: drowsiness risk difference 13.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 23.9); weight gain 6.9 (1.7 to 12.0).
analysis.covariates: None in the primary model. A prespecified adjusted analysis (baseline days of use, injecting, PHQ-9 score, age and sex) and multiple imputation by chained equations are said to leave the primary estimate unchanged, with numbers only in Supplement 3 (eFigure 2, eTables 7 to 9, not read) (Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, p. 585).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ANZCTR ACTRN12622000235707, described as prospectively registered; the protocol was published (Trials, 2024; reference 14) and is Supplement 1, and the statistical analysis plan is Supplement 2; the article states that all analyses were prespecified in that plan (Methods › Trial Design, p. 582; Statistical Analysis, p. 584). The registry record, protocol and analysis plan were not read, so registered and reported outcomes have not been compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Supplements 1 to 4 were not read. Sensitivity, adjusted and subgroup estimates, model details, other substance use and the full adverse-event tables are only in Supplement 3. No outcome after the 12 weeks of treatment is reported. Adherence is not reported by arm.
analysis.power: 340 participants for 90% power to detect a rate ratio of 0.75 on the primary end point (two-sided α .05), assuming 75% follow-up at week 12, with the effect size taken from Coffin et al. (2020) (Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584). The observed rate ratio (0.89) is smaller than the planned minimum; follow-up (86%) was better than assumed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Self-reported use fell more on mirtazapine: 2.2 days of 28 (95% CI 0.2 to 4.2) fewer than on placebo at week 12 (rate ratio 0.89), with smaller, non-significant differences at weeks 4 and 8. Both groups still used on about 16 to 17 of 28 days at week 12 (editors' calculation). The one drug-test measure did not differ (12.0% vs 13.2% of oral-fluid samples negative), nor did depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour or quality of life. Drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine, and 23% vs 15% stopped the medication for reasons related to it. No follow-up after treatment is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points conclude "Mirtazapine is safe and effective when used in routine clinical practice" (p. 582), and the Discussion says the trial confirms the phase 2 benefits and generalizes them to routine practice and a broader population (pp. 586–587). The Discussion fairly calls the effect diluted compared with the phase 2 trials (p. 587), but it cites strong agreement between self-report and biological measures, including in this trial, without addressing the oral-fluid result that showed no difference between arms (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, p. 587); the Results describe secondary end points as trending towards benefit although their intervals are centred near zero (p. 585); and the Discussion infers a direct effect on addictive processes from the absence of effects on depression and insomnia, without a mediation analysis (p. 587). 'Safe' rests on 172 people treated for 12 weeks.

timeline.event: Colfax et al.: 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 60 men who have sex with men in San Francisco; risk ratio 0.57 for a methamphetamine-positive urine at 12 weeks. Steven Shoptaw, second author of this trial, is one of its authors.

Coffin et al.: 120 cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in San Francisco, 24 weeks of treatment and 12 weeks of follow-up; risk ratio 0.67 at 12 weeks. No author in common with this trial.
Naji et al. meta-analysis of the two San Francisco trials, cited by this trial as showing a 14% difference in methamphetamine-positive urine tests (not read).

This trial: 339 adults at six Australian public clinics, including women (37%) and people with depressive symptoms (49%); self-reported use days reduced (−2.2 of 28; rate ratio 0.89), the oral-fluid measure not different.

replication.where_it_stands: Three placebo-controlled trials point the same way on their primary measures of use: two from one San Francisco team on urine positivity in sexual-minority men, and this larger trial from a different team (one investigator in common with the first trial) on self-reported use days in a broader population. The effect is smaller in this trial, its one drug-test measure did not differ, and only the second San Francisco trial reports outcomes after the medication stopped.

funding.funder: Australian Government Medical Research Future Fund (grant 2007155); the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre is supported by the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing; Drs Degenhardt and Berk were supported by NHMRC Leadership grants (2016825 and 2017131). The funders had no role in design, conduct, data handling, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit. Placebo tablets were supplied by Syntro Pty Ltd (Methods › Procedures, p. 582; Article Information › Funding/Support and Role of the Funder/Sponsor, p. 588).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Article Information › Conflict of Interest Disclosures, p. 588): Drs McKetin, Turner, Degan and Christmass reported Medical Research Future Fund grants during the study; Dr Shoptaw reported medications for a different study provided by Alkermes, Gilead Sciences and Indivior during the study and personal fees from Clear Scientific outside the submitted work; Dr Clare reported personal consulting fees outside the work and support from a New South Wales Ministry of Health programme; Dr Dore reported grants from AbbVie and Gilead Sciences during the study; Dr Dean reported NHMRC grants during the study and owning shares in Medigrowth; Dr Arunogiri reported speaker honoraria and advisory board fees from Camurus and Indivior outside the work; Dr Degenhardt reported NHMRC grants; Dr Goodman-Meza reported grants from the National Institutes of Health, St Vincent's Hospital and UNSW outside the work; Dr Hayllar reported speaker fees from Camurus and Indivior, donated to a medical charity, outside the work; Dr Colledge-Frisby reported employment by the National Drug Research Institute, which has Australian Government core funds; Dr Berk reported an NHMRC grant during the study and many other research grants and honoraria (including from Janssen) outside the work, and two issued patents. No other disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Led from the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, UNSW Sydney, with clinicians from the six public clinics among the authors. Dr Shoptaw (UCLA) is second author and an author of Colfax et al. (2011), the first San Francisco trial; he is listed for concept and design and critical review here. No other author appears in the author lists of the two San Francisco trials (Colfax et al., 2011; Coffin et al., 2020, from their reference records). Mirtazapine is a generic drug; no industry funding of the trial is reported.

what_would_settle_it: An independent multi-site placebo-controlled trial in a broad population of people with methamphetamine use disorder, with a drug-test-verified primary outcome (for example urine-confirmed use days or abstinence), a check of blinding, adherence support, and follow-up of at least 6 months after the medication stops, powered for an effect of the size seen here (about 2 days in 28).

domains.note: Randomized 1:1 with stratification by sex and depression, and matching placebo tablets with all clinicians, researchers and investigators blinded, but the article does not describe how the sequence was generated or how allocation was concealed (protocol not read). Baseline characteristics were well balanced (Table 1), so the concern is only the missing description.

Double-blind; estimands use all available data whether or not participants stopped the medication or took the rescue dose. Five people randomized to placebo who never received medication (1.5% of those randomized) are excluded, which is unlikely to matter. Other treatment was open to both arms.
Week-12 data for 86% (88% vs 85%); mixed models use all assessments, and multiple imputation is reported to leave the primary estimate unchanged (numbers only in the unread supplement).

The primary outcome is self-reported to blinded researchers. Participants could have guessed their allocation from drowsiness (47% vs 33%) or weight gain (10% vs 3%), no blinding check is reported, and the objective oral-fluid measure showed no difference between arms (12.0% vs 13.2% negative). Self-report agreed reasonably with oral fluid overall (sensitivity 89%, specificity 83%), but agreement by arm is not reported.

Prospectively registered, with a published protocol and a statistical analysis plan; the primary end point (week 12) and the analysis are reported as prespecified. The registry record and the plan were not read, so this judgment rests on the article's statements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted, adequately sized pragmatic trial with low attrition and a prespecified analysis. The concerns are that the article does not describe allocation concealment, and above all that the only significant result is on a self-reported outcome while the one objective measure did not differ and side effects may have revealed allocation; a modest expectancy effect on self-report could account for a difference of about 2 days in 28. The trial can be cited for a small reduction in self-reported use over 12 weeks and for the frequency of drowsiness, weight gain and stopping; it cannot be cited for reduced use on drug tests, for effects after treatment, or for long-term safety.

key_findings.finding: 1267 people assessed, 344 randomized (172 to each arm); 339 received trial medication (167 placebo, 172 mirtazapine) and all 339 were analysed; the 5 not treated were all in the placebo arm (3 did not attend baseline, 1 incarcerated, 1 withdrew consent).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 581); Figure 1 (p. 583); Results › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: Sample: mean age 42.0 (SD 8.6); 126 women (37.2%); a PHQ-9 score of 10 or more at eligibility in 82 (49.1%) on placebo and 83 (48.3%) on mirtazapine; injecting 48.5% (placebo) vs 43.0% (mirtazapine); median 10 years of schooling; 179 (52.8%) unemployed; 136 (40%) with a prison history; mean 21 years of methamphetamine use; median 24 (IQR 17 to 28) of the past 28 days used at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 581); Table 1 (p. 584); Results › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 584–585)

key_findings.finding: Primary end point: mean days of use in the past 28 days at baseline 22.0 (95% CI 20.3 to 23.8) on placebo and 23.1 (21.3 to 24.9) on mirtazapine; change to week 12, −4.8 (−6.2 to −3.4) vs −7.0 (−8.5 to −5.6); treatment estimand −2.2 days (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02; incidence rate ratio 0.89 (0.80 to 0.98), which the authors express as 8 fewer use days per 100 possible days.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph; Table 2, Primary end point
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (baseline mean plus mean change; approximate because the changes are model estimates): about 17.2 days of use in the past 28 days on placebo and 16.1 on mirtazapine at week 12. The rate ratio equals the ratio of the two arms' week-12 to baseline ratios (16.1/23.1 divided by 17.2/22.0 = 0.89).

key_findings.finding: Other time points: treatment estimand −1.3 days (95% CI −3.3 to 0.6), P = .20, at week 4 and −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06, at week 8; average over the 12 weeks −1.8 (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03. The primary estimate is reported as robust to multiple imputation and to adjustment for baseline covariates, with the numbers only in Supplement 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Secondary end points at week 12, none significant: methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid samples 12.0% (placebo) vs 13.2% (mirtazapine), difference 1.3 percentage points (95% CI −4.7 to 7.2), P = .68; PHQ-9 change −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0), P = .77; AIS-5 −0.6 (−1.4 to 0.2), P = .13; HIV risk behaviour −0.3 (−1.0 to 0.3), P = .32; EQ-5D 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9), P = .66.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Secondary end points; Results › Secondary End Points

key_findings.finding: By depression at eligibility, use-days estimand −2.8 (95% CI −5.7 to 0.0) in people not depressed and −1.4 (−4.2 to 1.4) in people depressed; estimands described as similar by sex and by depression (interaction tests only in the supplement). Among people depressed at baseline, insomnia improved more on mirtazapine at week 12 (−1.2, −2.3 to 0.0; P = .04), and depression did not (−1.2, −2.8 to 0.5; P = .16).

Medication discontinued by 85 (25%): 36 (22%) on placebo vs 49 (28%) on mirtazapine (P = .14); for reasons related to the medication 25 (15%) vs 40 (23%). Eight took the half-tablet rescue dose (6 mirtazapine, 2 placebo). MEMS adherence median 52% (IQR 26% to 78%), 62% (40% to 81%) excluding periods after discontinuation. Week-12 data for 293 of 339 (86%).

Safety over 12 weeks (placebo vs mirtazapine): drowsiness 55 (33%) vs 80 (47%), P = .01; weight gain 5 (3%) vs 17 (10%), P = .01; nervous system disorders 78 (47%) vs 111 (65%), P = .001; investigations 8 (5%) vs 19 (11%), P = .03; any adverse event 145 (87%) vs 155 (90%); serious adverse events 11 (7%) vs 7 (4%), none judged related to the medication; suicide risk (C-SSRS screener 3 or more) 6 (4%) vs 5 (3%); suicidal ideation 11 (7%) vs 11 (6%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Safety; Results › Exploratory End Points
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: drowsiness risk difference 13.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 23.9); weight gain 6.9 (1.7 to 12.0).

key_findings.finding: In this trial, self-reported methamphetamine use over the past 3 days had 89% sensitivity and 83% specificity against methamphetamine-positive oral fluid.

Design: prospectively registered (ACTRN12622000235707), protocol and statistical analysis plan supplied; all analyses stated to be prespecified. Sample size of 340 for 90% power to detect a rate ratio of 0.75, assuming 75% follow-up; confidence intervals not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Design (p. 582); Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 583) and last paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the effect diluted compared with the phase 2 trials: an 8% reduction in the risk of use on a given day against a 14% reduction in methamphetamine-positive urine tests in the earlier trials, attributing the difference to a heterogeneous population with entrenched use, poor adherence and frequent discontinuation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations
key_findings.note: The 8% is an absolute difference (2.2 of 28 days); the relative reduction implied by the rate ratio is 11% (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract prints the primary result as a mean difference of 2.2 days with a 95% CI of −4.2 to −0.2 days: the point estimate is positive and lies outside its own interval. Table 2 and the Results give −2.2 (−4.2 to −0.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign slip in the Abstract; the result is a reduction of 2.2 days.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Discussion call the primary result an 8% reduction in the risk of methamphetamine use on a given day. The 8% is 2.2 of 28 days, an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points of days. The Discussion then compares the 8% with a 14% reduction in methamphetamine-positive urine tests in the phase 2 trials, a different outcome (the Introduction calls it a 14% difference). Editors' calculation: the relative reduction implied by the incidence rate ratio of 0.89 is 11%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of 8% with 14% mixes outcomes and possibly scales; claims should give the days and the rate ratio rather than an 8% reduction in risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives medication discontinuation due to adverse reactions as 25 of 167 (15%) on placebo vs 40 of 172 (23%) on mirtazapine with P = .19. Editors' calculation from these counts: P = .053 (chi-square) or .055 (Fisher's exact test), while the other P values in the table match their counts (for example all discontinuations, P = .14).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed P value is probably wrong; the excess of medication-related discontinuation on mirtazapine is borderline rather than clearly non-significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract says 40 (23%) discontinued mirtazapine due to adverse events vs 25 (15%) on placebo; the Results call these discontinuations for reasons related to the trial medication and Table 3 calls them due to adverse reactions. Figure 1 shows that most were people who chose to stop because they did not like the medication's effects or did not feel it was working (29 on mirtazapine, 19 on placebo), with adverse events or other health risks given for 10 and 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read the 23% vs 15% as stopping for reasons related to the medication, not as stopping for adverse events.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives baseline EQ-5D utility scores as median 0.92 (IQR 0.85 to 0.97), on a scale whose maximum is 1, but Table 2 reports mean changes of 1.3 (placebo) and 2.2 (mirtazapine) with an estimand of 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9), which cannot be on the same scale; the unit of the change is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quality-of-life result cannot be interpreted as printed; it is null either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is headed as the intention-to-treat estimand, but all estimands use the 339 who received trial medication; the 5 randomized participants who never received it, all in the placebo arm, are excluded.
reporting_issues.consequence: A modified intention-to-treat analysis; with 1.5% excluded it is unlikely to change the result.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the total with suicide risk as 11 (4%) of 339; editors' calculation: 11 of 339 is 3.2%.
